chapter: Handy, Bix and disputes over credit
title: Handy, Columbia's search, and his rebuttal of Negro priority claims
summary: He argues white bands came first on Broadway, cites the Creole band's visit, and attacks critics of his claim.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Handy. That's correct. That's where they kept the account. The original name was from Memphis, Tennessee. It was called Pace and Handy, the original friend. Now, this Negro recorded. After Ralph Pell. I think this man runs a southern music company today, if I'm not mistaken. After our big success on Broadway and rising, that was January the 15th, which we opened there. And the sensation we created was something that they had never heard of in 50 years on Broadway. Anyway, the Columbia company, trying to get somebody to compete with us, sent this Ralph Pell to New Orleans where they recorded every white band, every colored band. He found none playing the same music that we played. That's when he went to Memphis, Tennessee. And Handy had a reputation. They had the greatest colored band in the United States at this time. He traveled all over extensively, this colored band, yeah, with his orchestra. I think I played in the last record, one of his records. One of the, on tape, I played you one of his records. And you can see what he played. Now, it said that the Negroes came before us. I've also contradicted that. They came on March the 6th, the great Creole band. If they took the trouble to look up the New York papers, maybe you'll have them in Tulane, you'll have the voice of the deaf. You'll see that I'm telling the truth. And these communistic writers are lying about this jazz business. They were a favor. They stayed there two weeks. Now, this was one of the greatest Negro bands that they had in New Orleans. And the last ad would appear in around December the 27th in Variety. You'll ask me how I remember those things. When a man's gold is as much as I have been, don't take long for him to remember these things. If you've been crucified by a bunch of crumbs, nut men, parasites. I wouldn't call them men. Because if they were men, they would have came and talked to me, seen what I had to offer, then write what they want about me. But today, they tell me I played ragtime. And only in these records you'll find the pristine roots of jazz. They'll say we wanted the creators of this music. They'll say many other things about us. They'll ridicule us. I've been often talked upon as like I was a thief somewhere. That one book had that I think Charles Edward Smith in a book he wrote. He says, yes, the rocker says that the people was astounded at the small amount of musicians. They could get so much music out of it. He meant in a different way. That I had taken other people's music. Well, I have proved that the Negro didn't play this music. In a previous tape that you've taken from me. If anyone's honest and wants to study them things, they'll see where the Negro got their material.
